entries.clue: Extremely striking entertainment coming to an end (4-8)

annotation.surface: A review praising a spectacular performance as it reaches its finale.
annotation.walkthrough: A show-stopping number is so striking that the applause halts the performance, so the wordplay's 'coming to an end' echoes the literal origin of the phrase.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: a number so striking that applause halts the show, hence any extremely striking thing.

indicatorNotes.holds: the boy holds the ring inside him

annotation.surface: A young suitor clutching an engagement ring he means to offer shortly.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Ring' giving O is a staple: the letter is the shape of a ring, and the boy goes around it.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: something happening soon happens before long.

indicatorNotes.set up: in a down clue, setting a word up turns it to read upwards

blocks.note: set up in a down clue, so read upwards

annotation.surface: Stage instructions for arranging a friendly welcome at a performance.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Set up' looks like 'arrange', but in a down clue it asks for the word before it to be turned upside down.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: Othello is one of Shakespeare's tragedies, one instance of a play.

entries.clue: Reserve about an hour for plant (5)

indicatorNotes.about: the reserve goes around the hour

blocks.note: a sub(stitute) is a reserve player
HR is the abbreviation for hour

annotation.surface: Someone setting aside an hour of gardening time for a particular plant.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Reserve' reads as a verb, to set aside, but it is the noun: a substitute player, wrapped around the hour.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: a shrub is one kind of plant, woody and bushy.

annotation.definitionNote: the second definition names the thing the answer describes; one-way is adjectival in both

blocks.note: reads as 'cannot be refunded', but means cannot come back
a single, as opposed to a return

annotation.surface: Small print on a ticket that cannot be refunded.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Non-returnable' suggests a ticket you cannot hand back for a refund; the trick is that it cannot bring you back, being a single rather than a return.
annotation.definitionFit: Both senses: a one-way trip allows no return, and a one-way ticket is a single.

blocks.note: PL is the abbreviation for place, as in street names

annotation.surface: A burglar raiding the flat downstairs.
annotation.walkthrough: 'From' seems to belong with 'place below', but it belongs to the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: plundering a place means stealing from it, usually by force.

entries.clue: In arena, a fitting canteen service (inits) (5)

indicatorNotes.In: the answer sits in the words that follow

annotation.surface: Praise for a catering service that suits a stadium.
annotation.walkthrough: '(inits)' tells you the answer is made of initials: the body that runs canteens and shops for British forces.
annotation.definitionFit: The initials stand for Navy, Army and Air Force Institutes, the body that runs forces canteens.

annotation.definitionNote: the second definition describes the word as used in a phrase naming a type of surgery

blocks.note: a small hole in a door lock
the tiny incision used in minimally invasive operations

annotation.surface: The first incision of a present-day operation.
annotation.walkthrough: Both senses are about small openings: one in a door, the other the tiny cut of keyhole surgery.
annotation.definitionFit: Both senses: a keyhole is a small opening in a lock, and keyhole surgery is modern minimally invasive surgery.

indicatorNotes.heading off: the first letter, the head, comes off

blocks.note: the parent loses its first letter

annotation.surface: A substitute parent setting out on a journey.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Heading off' sounds like leaving, but it means removing the head, the first letter.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: choosing the other one means choosing the alternative.

annotation.surface: A music lesson on a brilliant piece for two players.
annotation.walkthrough: 'About' reads as 'on the subject of', but here it means the letters are turned about.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: educating someone is teaching them.

entries.clue: Snack has association with Kent resort (4,8)

blocks.note: a town on the coast of Kent, a county in south-east England

annotation.surface: A snack food tied to a seaside town in Kent.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is almost true: the sandwich takes its name from the Earl of Sandwich, whose title comes from the Kent town.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: a club sandwich, stacked in layers, is one kind of snack.

entries.clue: I curse about love to cause separation (7)

indicatorNotes.about: the curse goes around the love

blocks.note: to slate is to criticise harshly

annotation.surface: Someone swearing at their partner and driving them away.
annotation.walkthrough: To slate is British for to criticise harshly, standing in here for 'curse'; love is nil in tennis.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: isolating something causes its separation from the rest.

entries.clue: Tale about leader of militants, full of angry outbursts (6)

indicatorNotes.about: the tale goes around the letter
indicatorNotes.leader of: the leader is the first letter

annotation.surface: A story about a rebel commander whose followers keep erupting.
annotation.walkthrough: The comma splits the clue: the definition is the adjective phrase at the end, not the militants.
annotation.definitionFit: Extended sense: weather full of storms lends its word to a relationship full of angry outbursts.

entries.clue: Master crazy with love for outstanding musician (7)

indicatorNotes.crazy: the letters go crazy, out of order

blocks.note: love = zero in tennis, O, added to the fodder

annotation.surface: A master who is mad about a gifted musician.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Master' is itself nearly the definition, which hides that it is only the letters to be mixed.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: maestro, Italian for master, is the title given to a distinguished musician.

entries.clue: Some mob rid alliances of unions? (6)

indicatorNotes.Some: only some of the letters are used

annotation.surface: A gang cutting its ties with other groups.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface makes 'unions' sound like trade unions or pacts; the question mark flags that it means marriages.
annotation.definitionFit: Adjective sense: bridal describes weddings, the unions of the question-marked definition.

blocks.note: DR is the abbreviation for doctor
R is the abbreviation for right

annotation.surface: Someone asking whether a doctor pushing in is on the right side.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Barge' looks like a verb, to push rudely, but it is the noun: a flat boat. 'On' just places side after doctor.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: a dredger is a barge-like vessel fitted to scoop silt from riverbeds.

indicatorNotes.some: only some of the letters are used

annotation.surface: An instruction to put some of the large towels away in another cupboard.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Elsewhere' looks like an anagram signal after 'Stow', but the letters sit in order across the two words.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: bath sheets are the largest size of bath towel.

blocks.note: the surface reading: a formal salutation, the first words of a piece of correspondence
the setter's reading: the first character of a word, here the word that names what 'Dear sir' begins

annotation.surface: The start of a formal letter, trailing off after one initial.
annotation.walkthrough: Two examples of the answer: 'Dear sir' is how a letter opens, and L is the letter that opens 'letter'. Neither is the paper knife the answer usually names.
annotation.definitionFit: Pun: a letter-opener is a paper knife, but here both things in the clue open a letter.

blocks.note: slang for nonsense; the question mark flags the pun

annotation.surface: A wry question about food that seems fit for the bin.
annotation.walkthrough: Tripe, the stomach lining of cattle, is eaten; 'tripe' also means worthless talk, so it is rubbish you can eat.
annotation.definitionFit: Pun: tripe is cattle stomach eaten as food, and also slang for nonsense.

blocks.note: E is the abbreviation for Eastern

annotation.surface: A creature imported from somewhere in the East.
annotation.walkthrough: 'From' only joins definition to wordplay; E is the standard compass abbreviation.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: the eland is a large African antelope, one kind of animal.

indicatorNotes.New: the letters are made into something new

annotation.surface: A choice between paying fresh fees or buying something pre-owned.
annotation.walkthrough: 'New' and 'second-hand' look like opposites in the surface, but 'New' only tells you to rearrange the dues.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: used goods have had an owner before, so are second-hand.

indicatorNotes.cultivated: cultivating works the letters into a new form

annotation.surface: A gardener leaning over a crop he has grown.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Cultivated plant' reads as one phrase, but 'cultivated' is the anagram signal and 'plant' alone is the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: the thistle, a prickly weed and Scotland's emblem, is one kind of plant.

entries.clue: Soldier trapped by rising sea needs protection (5)

indicatorNotes.trapped by: the soldier is held inside the sea
indicatorNotes.rising: the sea comes up backwards, read in reverse

annotation.surface: A soldier caught by a rising tide who must be rescued.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Rising' is a reversal signal even in an across clue, where the setter just means read backwards.
annotation.definitionFit: Idiom: under someone's aegis means under their protection; the word began as the shield of Zeus.

entries.clue: Deriders, once out of order, thought again (12)

indicatorNotes.out of order: the letters are put out of their order

annotation.surface: Mockers who were once unruly but have since changed their minds.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Once' reads as 'formerly', but it is just letters in the fodder.
annotation.definitionFit: Word structure: the prefix re- means again, and considered means thought over, so the parts spell out the definition.
